title: Multiplicity of Stable Attractors in Disordered Neural Models
authors: Raffaele Marino, Roberto Livi, Antonio Politi
abstract: We show how large-deviation statistics allows one to obtain reliable estimates of the multiplicity of stable fixed-points in a model of neural ordinary differential equations previously employed in computational tasks. The result is obtained by developing a suitable perturbative method in the amplitude of the disorder. It turns out that for not-too-large coupling strengths there are no qualitative differences between the symmetric case, when the dynamics is a purely gradient evolution, and the asymmetric case, when limit cycles and chaos can, in principle, arise. The selection of this specific model is dictated by pedagogical reasons, but we are confident that the approach can be extended to other many-degree-of-freedom dynamical models characterized by different classes of random coupling matrices.
summary: This work analyzes how the number of stable fixed points in disordered neural networks changes as coupling strength increases. Using large-deviation statistics and perturbation theory, the authors predict that SFPs disappear through bifurcations at a critical coupling $g_c$. The findings establish a quantitative link between disorder structure and dynamical stability in these complex systems.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the multiplicity of stable fixed-points (SFPs) in disordered neural ordinary differential equation models.
main_result: For small coupling strengths, there are no qualitative differences between symmetric and asymmetric dynamics; SFP depletion occurs via saddle-node bifurcations at a critical coupling strength $g_c$.
method: The authors employ large-deviation statistics combined with a perturbative method in the disorder amplitude to estimate the number of stable attractors.
model_or_system: The model consists of N neurons governed by nODEs, featuring local double-well potentials and interactions mediated by a random coupling matrix $A$.
key_observables: Average fraction of SFPs ($P_N(g)$), the minimum value $u$ derived from correlated Gaussian variables, and the multiplicity index $h(g)$.
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($g$), disorder amplitude, and system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The perturbative method is reliable for small $g$, and asymptotic analysis relies on large-deviation theory approximations.
figures_summary: Figures show the sharp drop in SFP fraction vs. coupling strength (Fig. 1), comparisons between perturbative estimates and exact solutions near bifurcations (Fig. 2), and density estimations $ho_N(u)$ for different matrix ensembles (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework using large-deviation theory to calculate SFP multiplicity, applies this to specific disordered neural models (asymmetric vs. symmetric coupling), derives analytical forms for the distribution of minima $u$, and compares these predictions against numerical simulations across different coupling regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on classical dynamics, the analysis of stability boundaries, bifurcations, and the role of disorder in determining system attractors shares conceptual links with understanding phase transitions or localization phenomena in quantum many-body systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1. Fraction of PN(g) of SFPs as a function of g for several sizes. Solid curves are simulation estimates averaged over different matrices (10 for N ≤20, 2 for N = 25); shaded bands indicate the uncertainty on the mean (error bar on the average). Dashed curves are the perturbative predictions obtained by integrating the minima density.

Figure 2. For small g, the stable fixed point (blue, lower branch) is a descendant of the g = 0 sign pattern with x∗(k) i ≈−1, and the component drifts continuously as g in- creases. The unstable equilibrium branch (red) approaches the stable one and annihilates with it near g ≃0.4. In green (orange) is presented the stable (unstable) path computed using our perturbative method.

Figure 3. Main panel: the symbols denote numerical esti- mates of ρN(u) for N = 20. Data have been obtained by averaging over 1000 realizations of the matrix A. Full cir- cles, crosses, and squares correspond to the Ginibre ensem- ble, a uniform distribution of entries, and to the symmetric case, respectively. The solid curves identify the correspond- ing theoretical predictions. Inset: the triangles correspond to h(u) estimated as ln ρN/N +ln 2 for the Ginibre ensemble. The black and red solid curves correspond to the theoretical predictions for asymmetric and symmetric matrices, respec- tively.

Figure 4. Comparison between the perturbative theoretical prediction h(g) = ln 2 + ln[1 −Φ(uc(g))] (black solid line) and the rate extracted from direct numerical simulations in the large-N limit (red squares with error bars).

Figure 5. Number of stable fixed points (SFP) as a func- tion of the system size N, shown on a linear–log scale. Blue markers denote the mean SFP averaged over disorder real- izations, with error bars. The red line is a least-squares fit that confirms an exponential growth SFP ∼e0.159N.
